t: Neither Minimum nor Maximum — Pick the Middle
o: Given distinct positive integers, return any element that is neither the min nor the max, or -1 when none exists. In [3,2,1,4] the min is 1 and max is 4, so 2 or 3 are valid answers. With only [1,2] every element is an extremum, hence -1. Since n can be as small as 1 or 2, we must guard those cases. Any element other than the two extrema qualifies, so after identifying the extrema anything else works — no specific value is required.
k: An answer exists iff n >= 3 (values are distinct).
Sorting puts a valid answer at index 1 immediately.
A single min/max scan plus one more scan finds a non-extremum in O(n) without sorting.

a.i: After sorting distinct values, nums[0] is the minimum and nums[n-1] the maximum. If n >= 3, nums[1] is strictly between them and is a valid answer; otherwise return -1.
a.t: O(n log n) — dominated by sorting.
a.sp: O(n) for the sorted copy (or O(1) extra if sorting in place is allowed).

a.i: Find the minimum and maximum in one pass, then return the first element equal to neither. This achieves O(n) time and O(1) space, which matters if the array were huge or streamed.
s: One pass computes mn = min(nums) and mx = max(nums).
Second pass returns the first x with x != mn and x != mx.
If no such x exists return -1.

w: Either approach passes comfortably given n <= 100. Mention the O(n) version to show awareness of constants; the sort version is fine for an easy warm-up. Edge cases: n = 1 and n = 2 must return -1. A cute O(1)-space, O(1)-time trick for n >= 3: examine any three elements and return their median. Follow-up: return all non-extreme elements, or handle duplicates (then 'neither min nor max' needs a stricter definition).
